Krishnan visited Leh and Ladakh in August 2019, Char Dham (the four sacred Hindu Himalayan shrines) in May 2022, Amarnath and Kashmir in May 2024, Adi Kailash in June 2025, and Vaishno Devi in October 2025. While hilly roads are known to be prone to landslides, studies show that road construction—which the Himalayan region (and India as a whole) has seen a lot of in the last decade —can contribute to both their frequency and magnitude. In March 2025, researchers published a landslide susceptibility map for an 80-km stretch from Karnaprayag to Joshimath in Uttarakhand along National Highway 7, a mountainous corridor connecting Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. The study demarcated areas into five categories of susceptibility: very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. In the Himalayan region, road construction frequently involves cutting into steep slopes with complex geological and hydrological conditions, explained Satish Pandey, scientist F & head, Flexible Pavement Division, CSIR-Central Road Research Institute, under the Ministry of Science and Technology. items.title: When a child breaks the law, the law must not break the child: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna
items.summary: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna on Saturday stressed that the juvenile justice system must prioritise rehabilitation over punishment, observing that "when a child breaks the law, the law must not break the child." Justice Nagarathna was delivering the opening remarks at the National Annual Stakeholders Consultation marking ten years of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, held at the Supreme Court. Highlighting the challenges surrounding the treatment of children accused of serious offences, Justice Nagarathna observed, "The question of treating a child in conflict with law as an adult represents one of the most delicate fault lines in our criminal justice system." She emphasised that juvenile justice boards (JJBs) were not intended to function as miniature criminal courts and that the law recognised children's capacity for development and change. Flagging serious institutional shortcomings, Justice Nagarathna cited a November 2025 India Justice Report study showing that 55% of cases before JJBs across 18 States and two Union Territories remained pending in 2023. The study also found that 24% of responding boards were functioning without their full complement of members. Emphasising that disposal of proceedings alone could not determine the success of the juvenile justice system, she said, "After all, a disposed case is not necessarily a rehabilitated child." In his address, Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant called for dedicated wings of specialised defence counsel to represent children. He also advocated coordinated training of police, judicial officers and psychologists, filling probation officer vacancies and protecting children's digital privacy. The CJI released an e-compendium of landmark judgments concerning juvenile justice from 2015 to September 2026. items.title: AI liability and regulation for India's GCCs
items.summary: India’s Global Capability Centres (“ GCCs ”) have evolved significantly from their traditional back-office functions. They are increasingly developing and deploying generative and agentic AI, not to mention adopting the use of AI in several functions. The use of AI may raise questions under data protection, intellectual property, employment, consumer protection, cybersecurity and sector-specific laws, while the nature of the system itself may raise separate questions about autonomy, human oversight, decision-making and accountability. A GCC therefore needs to assess both the legal framework applicable to a particular AI system and the how it operates. An AI tool that assists an employee in a GCC to prepare a recommendation is different from a system that independently makes decisions and acts. Consequently, the risks associated with each also differ. Before deployment, a GCC therefore needs to understand why each AI system will be used and how the AI will operate, including the level of autonomy involved, the information and data on which the AI will rely for the output, the role of human oversight and the potential consequences of an inaccurate, biased or otherwise inappropriate output, particularly where the consequences affect individuals, whether because the output is to be depended on or the system/operation involves personal data or in financial decisions. Indian regulatory framework At present, India does not have standalone, comprehensive legislation that governs either the development or the use of AI. Instead, AI-related risks are addressed through existing legislation, sectoral regulation and policy frameworks. The India AI Governance Guidelines released by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (“ MeitY ”) in November 2025 suggest the continued application of existing laws to different AI-related risks. Consequently, the legal requirements applicable to an AI system depend on the particulars of the system itself. To illustrate: an AI system used for recruitment may raise questions concerning bias and discrimination at the time of selection, depending on the information used to train the AI. Similarly, an AI model trained using employee or customer information may give rise to obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the use of copyrighted material in training or developing an AI model may be subject to scrutiny under the Copyright Act, 1957. items.title: Reform or legislative overreach? How Maharashtra's amendment to its public trusts law reached Tata Sons' governance
items.summary: In 2025, Maharashtra amended its public trusts law to limit the number of lifetime trustees where a trust’s governing instrument does not specifically provide for their appointment, a change that has placed some of India’s largest business houses, whose controlling shareholders are public trusts in Maharashtra, under regulatory scrutiny. A trust is a fiduciary arrangement whereby a settlor transfers property to a trustee to hold and manage for the benefit of beneficiaries. Private trusts, created for ascertainable individuals or classes, are governed by the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and give the settlor considerable autonomy over trustee appointments, distribution of benefits and the trust’s operation. Public trusts, created for charitable or religious purposes benefiting the public, are regulated by state legislation and attract greater oversight. Even so, the settlor’s intentions, as expressed in the trust deed, remain paramount. The State’s role has traditionally been supervisory, ensuring the trust’s objects are honoured and preventing misfeasance, malfeasance and non-feasance rather than interventionist in the selection and composition of trustees. The legislative framework: Maharashtra’s public trusts regime The Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950 (the “Act”) provides for the registration of public trusts, the duties and powers of trustees, and the role of the Charity Commissioner. For decades, it has balanced the State’s interest in proper administration of charitable trusts with the autonomy of trusts to operate according to their founding documents. While Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 generally empowers civil courts to address disputes relating to public charitable trusts, Section 52 of the Act excludes Sections 92 and 93 for Maharashtra public trusts. Instead, the Charity Commissioner exercises both administrative powers (registration, supervision, inspection and direction) and adjudicatory powers over disputes concerning trust property, trustee appointments and accounts. This concentration of functions makes the Charity Commissioner a powerful authority over public trusts. items.title: Is there a right time to go in-house?
items.summary: For many attorneys, moving in-house is seen as a natural progression in a legal career. After spending several years in private practice, the opportunity to work closely with a business, take ownership of legal and business issues, and become part of commercial decision-making can be compelling. However, the decision is often framed around when to leave private practice, rather than what an attorney should have built before making the move. While an in-house role can offer a different kind of exposure and responsibility, the transition also represents a significant shift in the way an attorney works. The skills and experience that are valuable in private practice may not always be the same as those required in-house. This raises an important question: Is there a right time to go in-house? Answer: There is no single point in a lawyer's career that can be considered the right time to move in-house. The answer depends on the lawyer’s experience, the nature of the role and, importantly, what they are looking to achieve from the move. For someone who wants to develop deep technical expertise, private practice may provide an opportunity to work across multiple clients and matters and build a strong foundation. For someone who wants to develop a closer understanding of a business, an in-house role may become attractive earlier. What is important is that the move should be made for the right reason. Going in-house because a particular role offers a better title, compensation or perceived work-life balance may not necessarily translate into a more fulfilling career. An in-house attorney is still an attorney, but the nature of the role is different. The focus can move from advising multiple clients on specific matters to understanding a business, its risks, objectives and commercial priorities. The question is therefore less about the number of years spent in a law firm and more about whether the lawyer understands what they are moving towards. Question: What should a lawyer have built before making the move? Answer: This does not mean that they need to know everything. In-house roles often require attorneys to work across issues they may not have encountered previously. items.title: Keralam govt sanctions compensation for Muthanga police torture victim KK Surendran
items.summary: The Keralam government has sanctioned a compensation of Rs 12.5 lakh to KK Surendran for the police torture he suffered during the 2003 Muthanga agitation. The government order followed a favourable court order earlier this year, after Surendran’s 22-year legal battle . The Muthanga agitation was a land occupation struggle led by the Adivasi Gothra Maha Sabha at the Muthanga Wildlife Sanctuary in Wayanad in February 2003. items.title: Sixth POCSO case registered against Gem Granites chairman Veeramani
items.summary: The Greater Chennai Police have registered a sixth case under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act against Gem Granites chairman R Veeramani on Saturday, October 10, in connection with allegations of sexual abuse of minor girls. Police sources said on Sunday, October 11, that the fresh case was registered based on statements by two minors. According to The Hindu , the allegations made by the two minors were clubbed and investigated as one case. With the registration of the latest case, the police are investigating the alleged sexual exploitation of 10 minor girls across six POCSO cases against the octogenarian businessman. Veeramani has also been booked in a case of abetment of suicide involving a minor in 2004. The Special Investigation Team (SIT) registered the latest case following a complaint by a mother who alleged that her daughter was sexually abused when she was a minor. The child had earlier lived in Chennai before moving to another district. Investigators are expected to take custody of Veeramani in the second POCSO case for questioning. According to The Hindu, a senior police officer said, “We have filed a request in the designated court requesting custody of the accused for questioning in another case.” The police have also searched Veeramani’s residence on Lloyd’s Road in Royapettah, Chennai, based on specific information. Veeramani and his accomplices, Shanthi and Mahendra Simhan, were arrested on August 28. The arrests followed an investigation by the Greater Chennai Police’s Anti-Vice Squad, which reportedly found video evidence on a previously recovered pen drive. Veeramani and Shanthi were subsequently arrested in another related case on October 8 and lodged at Puzhal Central Prison. Veeramani and his associates were later detained under the Goondas Act. Police sources said the accused would be formally arrested in the remaining cases as the investigation progresses. The investigation is examining allegations that Veeramani’s associates facilitated the alleged abuse at a house rented by the businessman. The case first came to light on October 6, 2025, when a child rights activist approached the Chennai police with a pen drive containing video footage allegedly showing a minor girl being sexually assaulted. The police registered a case on October 7, 2025, but later sought to close the investigation after failing to identify the girl in the video. items.title: PM Modi, CM Vijay vow to work together for Tamil Nadu's growth
items.summary: Approve phase three of the Chennai Metro Rail, make Cauvery-Godavari river linking a national project, release over Rs 5,000 crore education funds without imposing any conditions — these were among the slew of requests Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay made to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Chennai on Sunday, October 11. The Chief Minister listed the demands with Prime Minister Modi seated right next to him on stage at the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, after the launch of the 15-km Poonamallee Bypass–Vadapalani section of Chennai Metro’s Phase II. CM Vijay listed seven infrastructure projects that he requested the Union government to grant sanction to on a priority basis: Six-laning of the Chengalpattu–Tiruchirappalli section of GST Road (NH-32) Six-laning of the Tiruchirappalli–Panjappur–Jayapuram–Karur stretch of NH-81 Six-laning of the Karur–Coimbatore stretch Elevated corridor from Madhavaram, Chennai, to Sholavaram on NH-87 High speed rail corridor between Chennai and Kanniyakumari High speed rail corridor between Chennai and Coimbatore Reconsider Madurai & Coimbatore Metro Projects Other demands include Cauvery-Godavari river linking be made a national project Release Rs 5,110 crore due to Tamil Nadu under the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), without imposing any conditions Tamil as the principal language in the proceedings of the Madras High Court The two leaders said they are committed to work together for the state’s development, emphasising cooperation between the Union and state governments as they inaugurated and launched infrastructure projects worth over Rs 13,000 crore across Tamil Nadu. Addressing the gathering after Vijay’s speech, Prime Minister Modi said, “Governments and political leaderships may change, but our commitment to the people of Tamil Nadu and the rapid development of this state remains unshakeable. Today, we take this journey forward together with Chief Minister Joseph Vijay.” The Prime Minister also said urban development was a priority and described urbanisation as an opportunity rather than a challenge. He noted that metro services had expanded to 25 cities from five in 2014, while India's metro network had grown from around 250 km to more than 1,100 km. The projects inaugurated and launched during the Prime Minister’s visit also included highway works worth around Rs 3,700 crore, the Karaikal-Peralam railway line, three railway flyovers in and around Coimbatore, and five redeveloped Amrit Bharat stations

items.title: ‘Dear DK’: Bengaluru residents form human chains, demand cancellation of flyover tenders
items.summary: Residents, young citizens and activists gathered in Indiranagar and Jayanagar on Saturday, October 10, to oppose the Karnataka government’s proposed elevated corridors, demanding the cancellation of tenders and a shift towards public transport and other traffic solutions. Organised under the banner of ‘Dear DK’, the protests saw people from different age groups and political backgrounds hold placards, posters and roses while forming human chains along roads marked for the proposed infrastructure. Residents and parishioners of Resurrection Church also joined the protest on 80 Feet Road, which is part of the proposed alignment. The demonstrations add to growing opposition to Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure Limited’s (B-SMILE) elevated corridor projects. Residents of Indiranagar, CV Raman Nagar and HAL have been opposing the proposed corridor between Old Madras Road and Silk Board Junction. In south Bengaluru, residents are resisting a proposed 18.5-km corridor from Ragigudda Junction to Kanakapura Road, which will be tolled. Pravar, an architect and organiser with Dear DK, said the group had three demands for Deputy Chief Minister DK Shivakumar: cancel the tenders for all 13 proposed elevated corridors, reallocate the budget to alternative projects, and follow due process in planning urban infrastructure. “Bengaluru has built 44 flyovers in the last 20 years. You can argue that not many of them have solved traffic, right? Before we spend so much money and so much time building more flyovers, we should explore more options,” he said. Pravar questioned the emphasis on private vehicles, arguing that infrastructure planning must account for pedestrians, public transport users and the social and economic activity along the proposed routes. “Our city is not built only for cars. Our city is built for people,” he said, adding that only 7% of Bengaluru's population travels by car, while the remaining 93% depend on other modes of transport. The group also questioned the lack of public consultation and accountability in the planning process. Pravar called for the government to dissolve B-SMILE and restore the powers of the Bengaluru Metropolitan Land Transport Authority (BMLTA). “The people who are managing this project, B-SMILE, are an unconstitutional body, right? They have no elected members. They don't even have a website,” he said. items.title: Why power banks in hold luggage pose such a risk
items.summary: Airline passengers are being warned not to pack power banks in their hold luggage ahead of the summer holiday travel period. Devices with rechargeable batteries, like mobile phones, laptops, tablets, and smartwatches can be plugged into power banks on the go, where charging sockets may not be available. However, power banks are not danger-free or environmentally friendly. The warning has come from the UK’s Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), which believes that many travellers still aren’t aware of the rules – or the fire risk. Passengers on UK flights must take power banks – and other items containing lithium batteries – with them into the cabin. They must never be used to charge another electronic device while on the plane. Additionally, only two power banks per person are allowed on a flight. Consider a scenario where you are about to take off on a flight. You have settled into your seat, started using your mobile phone, and put it in airplane mode. All of a sudden, an unusual hissing sound comes from your bag; smoke starts rising, and within seconds, there is a fire inside your luggage. This actually happened on a flight between South Korea and Hong Kong in January 2026, when a power bank caught fire in mid-air . The accident on this flight is not a rare occurrence; hundreds of fires, explosions and other safety incidents involving lithium batteries and power banks have been recorded by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The main reason for accidents involving power banks is the lithium-ion battery, the most common battery type used in them. The lithium-ion battery has a tendency to overheat, which can trigger a thermal runaway in which the temperature rises rapidly, leading to the battery’s explosion. Such an explosion can occur for many reasons, including poor design, manufacturing issues, and improper use. In 2017, a family in the UK woke to smoke filling their home. The cause of the fire was a power bank charger, plugged into an electrical outlet. It overheated and set itself ablaze. Their rooms were burned down. From a scientific point of view, the answer is obvious: heat is the sworn enemy of lithium-ion batteries. Each time you recharge or discharge a power bank, chemical reactions produce heat in the battery. items.title: Eerie calm to the violence of lathis: Walking through Delhi on October 9 and 10
items.summary: On October 9, as the sun gently set over central Delhi, the city fell into an unusually quiet lull. It was the day before the protests demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and a rollback of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. If it weren’t so dystopian, it might have been called calm. The road leading to the protest site at Jantar Mantar had been barricaded at both ends. New surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees every few hundred metres. From the speakers, a woman’s voice, unhurried and polite, warned people not to join the next day’s demonstration. Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita was in force, she said. Gatherings of five or more, slogans, and protest symbols were prohibited. Then the message played again, and again, in a continuous loop. Closer to Jantar Mantar, a policeman stood over a labourer as he welded four rows of metal barricades into one, so that no protester could drag them apart. On October 9, new surveillance cameras and loudspeakers were strapped to trees and electric posts every few hundred metres Metal barricades were welded together so that protesters could not drag them apart Jantar Mantar is not where the Prime Minister lives. It is not where Gyanesh Kumar lives or where the Election Commission sits. It is simply the place the government itself set aside for dissent. Over time, this site has become where India brings what it cannot take anywhere else. For anyone with a prayer, a petition, or a protest, all roads usually lead to Jantar Mantar. But, on the eve of this protest — no roads led to Jantar Mantar. Instead, the entire city was swarming with thousands of security personnel. Hundreds of trains were cancelled. The borders of the capital were sealed. More than 50 metro stations were shut, and the traffic that remained was watched closely. The internet was going to be suspended in central Delhi the next day. The Delhi police made it clear that they had not granted permission for the protest. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) responded by saying they only informed the police. “We’ve been brainwashed all these years to think that to protest against the government, we need their permission first.
